groups.name: Pair I · C major (new)

pieces.title: Prelude I · Praeludium per omnes tonos
pieces.notes:
BWV 846's broken chords climb through all 24 keys in the WTC's own order, C, c, C#, c#, D, d and on to b, then home. In every minor key the Neapolitan chord (bII) becomes the next major tonic, a semitone up.

It is voiced as a Shepard-Risset illusion: each note sounds in several octaves under a fixed loudness curve, so the music rises a semitone with every key and yet arrives back in C at the register where it began. C minor opens with the Royal Theme of the Musical Offering. E-flat minor is the darkest point; the climax is a pedal in G-sharp minor; A major is the loudest bar.

At the da capo the fugue subject floats above Bach's own bars at half speed, the way Gounod laid a melody over this prelude. Try the meantone tuning: the remote keys sour, which is why the well-tempered keyboard existed.

pieces.title: Fugue I · Scala strettarum (2 voices)
pieces.notes:
The subject was found by search so that it combines with itself in stretto at every distance from a whole bar down to a single eighth note. The fugue climbs that ladder one rung at a time: bar, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and finally 1 eighth apart, through A minor, E minor, G, D minor, F and back to C.

Bach's own C-major subject (BWV 846) opens the piece alone in the bass and becomes the countersubject. It returns over the subject's augmentation in the coda, and B-A-C-H is the top line of the last cadence.

groups.name: Pair II · C minor (rebuilt, formerly 'Pair I')

pieces.title: Prelude II · the beat lost and found
pieces.notes:
The left hand keeps a steady quarter-note beat while the right hand's sixteenths regroup in 4s, then 3s, then 5s. The accented first note of each group spells out the fugue subject, first in long values, then in E-flat starting a sixteenth late. The written-out Presto and Adagio in bars 23-24 come from BWV 847's prelude, before the downbeat returns. It ends on C5, the fugue's first note.

Fixed from v3: the chord chart filled by a voicing optimiser, the lack of any melody, and the sagging dominant pedal.

pieces.title: Fugue II · three voices (was two)
pieces.notes:
Renumbered to No. II, as in Bach's key order, so it now has three real voices like BWV 847. The exposition has the answer as the subject's mirror image at the dominant, then the bass entry with two countersubjects. In G minor the subject sounds together with its augmentation and its inversion. Then the whole three-voice block returns upside down in F minor, a mirror trio in the manner of Contrapunctus 12/13.

The peak is now the fullest bar, a three-voice stretto half a bar apart. A deceptive cadence and a Neapolitan follow. In the coda Bach's own BWV 847 subject enters slowly in the bass under ours.

Every note was written by hand; the old version had 15 bars of code-chosen pitches. 0 parallels, 0 unresolved dissonances, playable by two hands.

groups.name: Pair III · C-sharp major (new fugue, prelude repaired)

pieces.title: Prelude III · Glass bells
pieces.notes: The second-draft prelude Sam liked, transcribed note for note, with four repairs: outer-voice fifths across the barline at bar 12, inner layers that doubled the melody at bar 20, outer-voice octaves into the cadential 6/4 at bar 21, and a major-seventh leap at bar 5. The bells, the silences and the harmony are otherwise untouched; a final ritardando is added. The deep bass is meant to be caught with the middle (sostenuto) pedal.

pieces.title: Fugue III · Giga a 4, rectus et inversus
pieces.notes:
A four-voice gigue-fugue in 12/8. As in Bach's suite gigues, Part 1 presents the subject upright and cadences in G-sharp, and Part 2 presents it upside down, with the entries in mirrored order: bass, tenor, alto, soprano.

In the coda (bars 40-41) the gigue meets its own reflection: bars 9-10 of Part 1 sound simultaneously with bars 23-24 of Part 2, at pitch. The countersubject was designed backwards from this moment so that the four lines fit.

Bach's own C-sharp-major subject (BWV 848) appears too: the soprano's inverted subject ends G#-A#-G#, which is the head of Bach's subject, so it runs straight on into it (bars 28-29).

groups.name: Pair IV · C-sharp minor (rebuilt)

pieces.title: Prelude IV · Allegro inquieto
pieces.notes: The motif, its syncopation, augmentation, diminution and hemiola are kept. New in this version: root-position cadences at the return and the close, the hands imitating each other at the half bar, and a dominant pedal that moves every half bar. Bach's BWV 849 'cross' motif (C#-B#-E-D#) is planted as 4-3 and 6-5 suspensions over that pedal, so the prelude previews the fugue's second subject.

pieces.title: Fugue IV · double fugue with Bach's cross
pieces.notes:
Five voices that build up and stay; all five first sound together at bar 10 (bar 33 before). The countersubject now has one fixed shape.

Bach's own stile-antico subject from the five-voice C-sharp minor fugue BWV 849 (C#-B#-E-D#) becomes a genuine second subject. It has a quiet second exposition in bars 17-25 with Bach's own answer, appears in diminution in the episode basses, and at the climax (bars 35-41) sounds augmented in the bass under two complete strettos of our subject an eighth apart. The final stretto is in three voices over the dominant pedal.

Accented parallels down from 22 to 1; tripled pitch classes down from 19% to 8%.

groups.name: Pair V · D major (rebuilt)

pieces.title: Prelude V · Allegro
pieces.notes: The climb and climax of the old version are kept. New: an irregular 6+8+6+12+6+3-bar form instead of five identical 8-bar blocks, a B-minor region, and a written top line over a walking left hand. The fugue's head cell and tattoo rhythm pass between the hands. It ends with a 32nd-note flourish that becomes the fugue subject in diminution and runs straight into the fugue, as BWV 850's prelude does.

pieces.title: Fugue V · six voices, cascade stretto
pieces.notes:
The trumpet-and-drum subject is kept, now with a tonal answer, a syncopated countersubject and uneven entry spacing. Middle entries in B minor and E minor (inverted). The strettos no longer sit on a held triad: in G the subject combines with its diminution and inversion over a walking bass, and in E minor the inversion enters off the beat.

The climax is a cascade stretto: six entries from soprano down to contrabass, one bar apart and each a fifth lower, through F#m, Bm, Em, A, D, G. Bach's own D-major subject (BWV 850) then enters as a genuine baritone voice. The subject appears at four speeds (x4, x2, x1, x1/2) in bars 47-54, at most three at once. The tonic pedal is coloured with C natural and B flat, and the timpani play the tattoo.

Accented parallels down from 38 to 0; tripled pitch classes from 38% to 9%.

groups.name: Pair VI · D minor (new, seven voices)

pieces.title: Prelude VI · Toccata con recitativo
pieces.notes: Opens with the famous gesture of the Toccata in D minor BWV 565 in octaves, then runs in the triplet figuration of WTC I's D-minor prelude (BWV 851) over the fugue's ground. Two recitatives interrupt it, declaiming the fugue subject's pitches in free rhythm: first in the right hand, then in the bass. It stops on a half cadence, with the 565 figure breaking off on C sharp, and the fugue begins on the missing D.

pieces.title: Fugue VI · Passacaglia e fuga a 7
pieces.notes:
The ground is the chromatic lament of Bach's Crucifixus (BWV 232 / BWV 12), moved to D minor: D C# C B Bb A, Bb G A D. The fugue subject is that ground upside down at double speed, so ground and subject are relatives.

As in the middle of the Passacaglia BWV 582, the ground migrates. It passes from the bass to the second tenor, the first tenor (in F major), the second alto (A minor), the first alto (G minor), the second soprano (back in D minor) and the first soprano (on the dominant), freshly harmonised each time.

At the summit (bars 49-64) the ground sounds at three speeds at once: augmented in the bass, at double speed in the alto, and at normal speed in the soprano. Meanwhile the subject enters in stretto in the inner voices, arriving on D major. The coda puts B-A-C-H in the alto over a D pedal.

After a second review the tempo is a steady quarter = 76, a running voice drives each later variation, the ground is brought forward at every new station, and the script-proposed passing notes that clashed were removed.

groups.name: Pair VII · E-flat major (new, eight voices)

pieces.title: Prelude VII · Chorale prelude on Wachet auf
pieces.notes: Philipp Nicolai's chorale 'Wachet auf, ruft uns die Stimme' (1599), the tune of Bach's Schübler prelude BWV 645, which is also in E-flat major. As in BWV 645, the chorale sounds in long notes in the tenor. The dancing obbligato above it is the fugue subject in diminution, so the prelude secretly previews the fugue. The chorale's last line is answered by its own mirror image while the bass plays the diminished subject and then its inversion.

pieces.title: Fugue VII · Fuga a due cori
pieces.notes:
Two complete four-voice choirs, after Gabrieli's and Schütz's cori spezzati and Bach's double-choir motet Singet dem Herrn (BWV 225). The subject opens with the first line of Wachet auf. Choir II sings a literal mirror image of Choir I's whole exposition, as in the Art of Fugue's mirror fugues. The choirs then trade at shrinking distances: a bar, half a bar, a beat.

In bars 25-29 the choirs disagree about the key, Choir I insisting on B-flat and Choir II on A-flat, until they reconcile on the home dominant. Then a joke: Choir I's pompous augmentation is cut off twice by Choir II's chattering diminution, and its last bar only arrives in the coda.

The summit is an eight-voice stretto, every voice entering half a bar apart, Choir I upright and Choir II inverted. In the binaural render Choir I is on the left and Choir II on the right.

groups.name: Pair VIII · E-flat minor (rebuilt, nine voices)

pieces.title: Prelude VIII · Night loom
pieces.notes: Rebuilt on the 12/8 'Night loom' prelude from the first complete draft, which Sam liked, in place of the French overture that had replaced it. The melody is the fugue subject played backwards and upside down; the woven eighth-note figure changes shape almost every half bar. The bass ends with the subject's head and stops on the dominant, so the fugue's first note completes it.

pieces.title: Fugue VIII · nine real voices
pieces.notes:
The subject's first six notes are the head of Bach's D-sharp-minor fugue subject (BWV 853), now credited. All nine voices enter in the exposition at shrinking distances, including a subject and its inversion one beat apart. The middle has augmentations, a 'dance' episode in which subject and countersubject run in sixteenths and thirty-seconds, and a false return in mirror image.

A chain of entries one beat apart climbs to a bar of silence. Then comes the arrival: one nine-voice chord whose every note begins a line, over the bass of the arrival Sam liked in the second draft, now singing the subject at quarter speed. Eleven more statements, upright, inverted and augmented, sound above it with all nine voices moving for seven bars. A deceptive cadence leads to a quiet C-flat interlude. Then Bach's complete subject enters as a guest under ours, with the prelude's melody in the bass.

Against the old 100-bar version: parallel fifths/octaves 218 -> 0, accented parallels 294 -> 0, low-register clashes 286 -> 11.

groups.name: Pair IX · E major (new, ten voices)

pieces.title: Prelude IX · Pastorale in just intonation
pieces.notes:
A 12/8 pastorale, after WTC I's E-major prelude, tuned note by note in pure 5-limit just intonation: every chord has pure thirds and fifths, and any note held or repeated across a chord change keeps its pitch. The tune's progression I-vi-ii7-V7-I then forces the pitch to sink by a syntonic comma (21.5 cents) every time round. This is the comma pump, the problem tempered keyboards exist to solve.

Four cycles of the theme each sit a comma lower, 86 cents down by the end, nearly a semitone. A low E that stays at well-tempered pitch is struck at the start of each cycle, so the drift can be heard as it beats against the drone: not at all, then about 2, 4 and 6 times a second. In the last breath the drone sounds alone, and the coda returns to agree with it at well-tempered pitch. Compare 'Prelude IX (tempered)' below, which has the same notes with no drift.

pieces.title: Prelude IX · same notes, well-tempered
pieces.notes: The pastorale with no per-note tuning: it follows the temperament buttons, so it never drifts. Use it for comparison with the just-intonation version above.

pieces.title: Fugue IX · Ricercar a 10 in circulo
pieces.notes:
Ten voices in stile antico, white notes and suspensions, imagined as a ring of singers in the manner of Tallis's 40-voice Spem in alium. The subject's held E is a built-in suspension. The exposition is one continuous build-up, each entry starting before the last has finished, moving round the circle of fifths. In the binaural render the entries literally travel round the listener.

The subject of Bach's WTC II E-major fugue (BWV 878), which Bach himself took from J.C.F. Fischer, enters as a real voice four times. It sounds augmented in the bass to make the first tutti, in Bach's answer form above it, in A major in the second choir, and augmented as the treble cantus firmus of the final tutti. As in Spem in alium, the first tutti is followed by a bar of silence, then antiphonal exchanges shrinking from four bars to half a bar. At the end the voices drop out in pairs around the ring, each touching its last note again softly as it leaves. The ring and its travelling entries are fully heard only in the binaural render.

groups.name: Pair X · E minor (new, eleven voices)

pieces.title: Prelude X · Aria e Presto
pieces.notes: After WTC I's E-minor prelude (BWV 855), an aria over a steady figure that breaks into a Presto. The aria paraphrases lines of the chorale 'O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig' over a chromatic lament ground and a walking eighth-note figure. The Presto is in two-part invertible counterpoint through E minor, B minor, A minor and G, then a canon and a dominant pedal. It stops on D sharp and runs straight into the fugue.

pieces.title: Fugue X · a due cori con corale
pieces.notes:
An homage to the opening chorus of the St Matthew Passion: two five-voice choirs, with the chorale 'O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig' (soprano of Bach's harmonisation BWV 401) floating above in long notes, phrase by phrase. The fugue subject's main notes are the chorale's first line moved down a third, so fugue and chorale are relatives.

Choir I's exposition is followed by a dialogue of fragments, 'Sehet! / Wen? / den Bräutigam / Wie? / als wie ein Lamm', in the manner of Bach's chorus. Choir II then gives a mirror exposition in inversion.

Under the chorale's last line the choirs swap forms in a final stretto, thinned so that each entry can be heard directly under the chorale; all eleven lines meet at the cadence. The eleven voices arrive at the last chord one or two per beat, each by step. In the binaural render Choir I is on the left, Choir II on the right and the chorale in front.

groups.name: Pair XI · F major (new, twelve voices)

pieces.title: Prelude XI · Invention a 2
pieces.notes: A two-part invention in 12/8, after WTC I's F-major prelude (BWV 856). The theme is the fugue subject with a triplet head; the countersubject is invertible at the octave and heard both ways round in six keys. The surprise: a half cadence on a lone 'C C', answered by the theme in D-flat major. It ends by stating the fugue's opening 'C C | F' straight, in sixteenths.

pieces.title: Fugue XI · Concerto fuga a 12
pieces.notes:
After the fugal finale of Brandenburg Concerto No. 2 in F major (BWV 1047): a concertino of four solo lines (named Tromba, Flauto, Oboe, Violino) against a ripieno of eight separate real lines. The subject is a fanfare head with repeated notes and a running tail. Its inversion keeps the F-major triad, so the upright and inverted subject can run in stretto a beat apart.

The joke (bars 41-47): the trumpet keeps hammering its tattoo on C while everyone else modulates away, through C minor, F, D minor and A, landing in E major. The trumpet then blurts its head in F, a semitone off everything. General pause. The band holds its E chord, the bass corrects the trumpet (E E | A), and the trumpet echoes meekly. Its tattoo returns on C over the final dominant, where C is finally right.

The 'tutti in twelve' (bars 53-57) has a concertino stretto a beat apart, the inversion augmented in the violone, inversions in the inner ripieno, and the countersubject four times in diminution, with 10-11 of the twelve lines moving in every bar.

groups.name: Pair XII · F minor (new fugue, thirteen staves)

pieces.title: Fugue XII · Fuga a 4 soggetti, compiuta
pieces.notes:
The Art of Fugue breaks off in its last fugue just after the third subject, B-A-C-H, has joined the first two. In 1880 Gustav Nottebohm showed that the three subjects also combine with the work's main theme, so Bach evidently planned a quadruple fugue. This fugue completes that plan, moved to F minor and expanded to thirteen staves, using Bach's exact subjects.

Section I is the first subject in stile antico, gathering voices. Section II brings the running second subject, first alone and then combined with the first. In Section III, B-A-C-H enters in stretto pairs, then Bach's own triple combination from the unfinished fugue (transposed), a lament bass and a half-bar of silence. Section IV gives Nottebohm's quadruple combination, the same combination upside down, and a stretto finale with the first subject augmented in the bass and at three speeds at once. In the coda, the literal B-flat-A-C-B-natural signature sounds over the tonic pedal, and its A becomes the Picardy third.

Second version, still short of its aim: at its fullest ten of the thirteen voices sound at once (over a four-bar dominant pedal before the finale), and the B-A-C-H section carries about six.

groups.name: Pair XIII · F-sharp major (new, fourteen voices)

pieces.title: Prelude XIII · Aria
pieces.notes: A 16-bar ornamented sarabande over the Goldberg ground, the bass on which Bach built all thirty Goldberg Variations, here in F-sharp major. Like the Aria that opens the Variations it is decorated with turns, appoggiaturas and written-out trills, but its melody is new.

pieces.title: Fugue XIII · Fuga canonica a 14 sopra il fondamento di Goldberg
pieces.notes:
Every third Goldberg Variation is a canon, at the unison, the second, the third and so on up to the ninth, and Bach later wrote fourteen more canons on the same ground (BWV 1087). Here the ground runs ten times in F-sharp, and with each round a new canon pair enters and stays: at the unison, the second, the third, the fourth and fifth by inversion, and the sixth. The subject is the ground itself in dotted diminution.

At the summit (bars 57-64) all six canons sound together over the ground with the subject in stretto. Then, as in the Goldberg's Variation 30, a quodlibet: the two folk songs 'Ich bin so lang nicht bei dir g'west' and 'Kraut und Rüben' (checked against Bach's Variation 30), here in canon themselves and in augmentation, ending on a fourteen-voice chord.

First version: at the summit 9-12 voices sound at once, and several voices rest until the final chord.

groups.name: Fugue XIV · F-sharp minor (new, fifteen voices)

pieces.title: Fugue XIV · Ricercar a 15 sopra il Thema Regio
pieces.notes:
In 1747 Frederick the Great gave Bach a theme to improvise on. Bach managed a three-voice fugue on the spot and later wrote the six-voice Ricercar and the canons of the Musical Offering. This ricercar takes the Royal Theme, checked against Bach's text and moved to F-sharp minor, to fifteen voices in three choirs.

The first choir enters one voice at a time, then comes the Musical Offering's canon by augmentation and contrary motion (the theme against its inversion at half speed). The middle section is a canon per tonos, after Bach's canon that rises a tone with each repetition 'so may the King's glory rise': a four-bar canonic block heard in F-sharp, G-sharp, A-sharp, C, D and E minor, its leading voice climbing a step each time and gaining a line with each statement. In the fourth statement the theme sounds at Frederick's own pitch, from middle C. The seventh step returns to F-sharp minor and is the summit: the theme and both countersubjects in augmentation, against the theme and countersubject in diminution, with the inversion on top. It ends on a fifteen-voice Picardy chord.

Still short of its aim: at the summit about ten of the fifteen voices move at once, and the quarter-note canon tends to sound like the theme in thirds.

groups.name: Pair XV · G major (new, four voices)

pieces.title: Prelude XV · Musette
pieces.notes: A short 12/8 shepherds' musette over a drone, alluding to the first line of Luther's Christmas chorale 'Vom Himmel hoch'. Bar 13 quotes the flutes' shepherd music from Part II of Bach's Christmas Oratorio (BWV 248).

pieces.title: Fugue XV · on 'Vom Himmel hoch' (4 voices)
pieces.notes:
Bach's Canonic Variations on Luther's Christmas chorale 'Vom Himmel hoch' (BWV 769) end with all four lines of the chorale sounding at once. Here each of the four voices owns one line, and that line becomes its fugue subject: a dotted skip ending in bells (soprano, line 1), a fanfare (tenor, line 2), a siciliano (alto, line 3) and falling bell-rounds (bass, line 4). Each voice also sings its own line once in long notes.

The subjects enter in the chorale's order, each paired with the one before, and each section ends in a new key: D, E minor and B minor, C, home to G. At the summit (bars 43-48) only the four chorale lines sound, each entering alone in its own register, all four together for about ten beats. In the coda the four subjects' heads ring together, and the soprano closes on B-A-C-H.

Recomposed in four voices (it was sixteen); the earlier version is in the pair's archive folder.

groups.name: Pair XVI · G minor (new, seventeen voices)

pieces.title: Prelude XVI · Fantasia
pieces.notes: A short organ fantasia in four sections: a flourish over a G pedal (its first two beats allude to the opening of Bach's G-minor Fantasia BWV 542), a recitative with a Neapolitan sixth, the first line of the chorale 'An Wasserflüssen Babylon' over a falling chromatic bass, and a close over a D pedal that stops on the dominant, waiting for the fugue.

pieces.title: Fugue XVI · Fantasia e fuga a 17 per Reincken
pieces.notes:
In 1720 Bach improvised for nearly half an hour on the chorale 'An Wasserflüssen Babylon' in Hamburg, before the old organist Johann Adam Reincken, who told him: 'I thought this art was dead, but I see that it lives on in you.' This fugue re-imagines that improvisation for seventeen voices on three manuals and two pedal divisions.

Each of the chorale's ten lines gets its own fugal subject made from its own notes, introduced in the manuals; then the line itself sounds in half notes as a canon at the octave between the two pedal voices, the canon's distance shrinking from ten beats to three. Between lines: an echo passage across the manuals, a general pause, a lone arpeggio. Just before the summit, the subject of Bach's own G-minor organ fugue (BWV 542, the piece often linked with that Hamburg visit) enters as the pedal bass, landing on the summit's first downbeat. At the summit the last chorale line runs in the pedal canon under seventeen subject statements, and a tonic-pedal coda ends on G major with all seventeen voices.

First version: outside the five-bar summit the texture is mostly three to five moving voices.

groups.name: Fugue XVII · A-flat major (new, eighteen voices)

pieces.title: Fugue XVII · Fuga, fuggendo la cadenza (18 voices)
pieces.notes:
Zarlino called an evaded cadence 'fuggire la cadenza', to flee the cadence, the same root as fugue. A story told about Bach (probably a legend) has his children getting him out of bed by playing an unresolved chord on the harpsichord: he could not sleep until he had gone down and resolved it.

In this fugue every cadence is evaded, and each evasion lets in a new voice. A chain of deceptive cadences, each landing a third lower, drifts far from home, to A-flat minor and a dreamlike E major with the subject in augmentation, then turns back. At home the evasions get more desperate: after the dominant the bass slides to F, F-flat, G-flat, A-flat under a minor chord. Finally all seventeen 'children' stop on a dominant seventh with D-flat on top, and wait.

The eighteenth voice, the father, enters alone. The hanging D-flat falls to C as he sings the subject in augmentation, and his bass gives the piece its first perfect cadence. The subject of Bach's own A-flat fugue in Book I (BWV 862) appears as a guest at its own pitch.

groups.name: Pair XVIII · G-sharp minor (new, nineteen voices)

pieces.title: Prelude XVIII · Der Wächter
pieces.notes: The watchman. The right hand sings the fugue's subject over a knocking middle voice and a walking bass; at 'midnight' the middle voice plays the whole of the fugue's second subject, the knock at the door. It ends on an open fifth with three knocks that nobody answers.

pieces.title: Fugue XVIII · Vigilate (19 voices)
pieces.notes:
'Watch therefore, for ye know not when the master of the house cometh: at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning' (Mark 13:35). The fugue passes through those four watches. In each watch one note of the subject is raised, in the order sharps are added to a key signature, so the subject brightens step by step from a dark Phrygian colour towards major. The last step would need an eighth sharp, impossible in G-sharp, so the dawn turns enharmonically to A-flat major, the key of the next pair.

The second subject is the knock at the door, from Bach's cantata 'Nun komm, der Heiden Heiland' BWV 61, where the bass sings 'Siehe, ich stehe vor der Tür und klopfe an' (Behold, I stand at the door and knock): three knocks, then a chromatic rise through exactly the notes that change between the watches. Like Bach's G-sharp-minor fugue in Book II, this is a double fugue with a chromatic second subject.

At the first summit eight entries of the subject climb in thirds, two beats apart, from G-sharp2 to G-sharp5. At the second, four statements of the door subject sound in stretto over a knocking pedal, with knocks relayed between voices (16-18 voices moving); eighteen voices knock together, a silence, then the dawn in A-flat major, the voices waking one by one.

groups.name: Pair XIX · A major (new, twenty voices)

pieces.title: Prelude XIX · Le Maître à danser
pieces.notes: The dancing master shows the steps: allemande, courante, sarabande and gigue, twelve beats each, then pairs of them at once in different metres, then the first three bars of a Bach bourrée at pitch, which turns out to matter in the fugue.

pieces.title: Fugue XIX · Ballo a quattro cori (20 voices)
pieces.notes:
A Baroque suite is a chain of dances, often built on one melody. Here four five-part string bands, scored like the court band of Lully's France, each own one dance: allemande (4/4), courante (3/2), sarabande (3/4) and gigue (12/8). One subject is re-rhythmed for each dance, and each band gets its own fugal exposition.

Then the dances meet: two at once, then three, and at the summit all four together, each in its own metre, sharing one beat, their bar lines coinciding only every twelve beats. That is the trick of the ballroom scene in Mozart's Don Giovanni, here in strict counterpoint. Only one band's bass plays at a time: the subject's mirror passes from band to band as the bass, faster each time.

In the coda the subject reveals where it came from: the opening of the Bourrée I from Bach's English Suite No. 1 in A major (BWV 806), which the allemande band plays with Bach's own bass before all twenty voices close on A. Solo one band in the listening room to hear each dance on its own.

groups.name: Pair XX · A minor (new, twenty-one voices)

pieces.title: Prelude XX · Preludio for solo violin
pieces.notes: A single line in perpetual motion, as in Bach's solo-violin preludes; one hand can play it at the keyboard. The first bar hides the head of the fugue's subject inside the figuration, and the lament and the fugue's tail are foreshadowed. (The renders folder also has a violin-sound version.)

pieces.title: Fugue XX · Fuga per un violino solo, moltiplicata (21 voices)
pieces.notes:
Bach's Sonata No. 2 for solo violin in A minor (BWV 1003) contains a fugue for one violin: a single line that, by leaping between registers, implies three or four voices. This fugue begins exactly like that, a solo violin fugue on the head of Bach's subject.

Then the hidden voices come out. Wherever the violin's line is really two strands, a new string player catches one strand at the exact sixteenth and carries it on as a real voice, so each new voice is something you have just heard implied. The new voices in turn imply further strands, which split off again, violins, violas, cellos, basses, until twenty-one real voices move at the summit, over the subject in four-fold augmentation in the double bass (19-21 voices moving in every bar).

Then the process reverses: over the summit's lament as a ground, voices fold back into the lines they came from, in reverse order, until the violin is alone again, implying the whole harmony by itself, as in the Chaconne. Its last A is the last sound. In the listening room it plays on one keyboard sound; the rendered MP3 gives each voice a string instrument.

groups.name: Pair XXI · B-flat major (new, twenty-two voices)

pieces.title: Prelude XXI · Arioso
pieces.notes: After the young Bach's Capriccio on the Departure of a Beloved Brother (BWV 992), whose friends first try to coax the traveller into staying. The friends' theme in Bach's sixths, a lament bar over Bach's own chromatic lament bass, a posthorn call in the distance, and a farewell.

pieces.title: Fugue XXI · Capriccio sopra la lontananza (22 voices)
pieces.notes:
Bach's Capriccio ends with a 'fugue in imitation of the postilion's horn'. A natural posthorn can only play the harmonic series of its fundamental, so here the twenty-two voices are the first twenty-two partials of B-flat: voice n lives around partial n. The horns state a posthorn subject made only of partials (Bach's head, then a climb up the series); the friends answer with a theme built on Bach's Arioso, which reaches G, the one note the horn can never play.

Seven 'strangers' play Bach's real subject in foreign keys. Where Bach writes G, each horn cracks to its out-of-tune 7th partial, a minor seventh 31 cents flat, the friends laugh, and the crack pulls the music one fifth round the circle. The climb passes a lament bar, the post station, Bach's Aria with the alphorn's 11th partial (49 cents flat) and rockets in stretto. At the summit Bach's whole subject sounds in the bass with the posthorn subject twice and the friends' theme in stretto (18-19 voices moving).

The departure: a farewell in the Arioso's sixths, then a relay in which each voice settles on its own partial, until the last sound is the posthorn's own harmonic series, partials 1 to 22, tuned exactly, nature's B-flat over the well-tempered one. The first horn plays the subject's head once more, very softly.

The cracks and the final chord carry their own tuning, so the temperament buttons do not apply to this piece.

groups.name: Pair XXII · B-flat minor (new, twenty-three voices)

pieces.title: Prelude XXII · Tombeau
pieces.notes: A tombeau, the French lament for the dead, after Froberger and Louis Couperin (their manner, not their notes), written out in measured notation with a free tempo. A gathering chord, the head of Bach's B-flat-minor fugue in Book I, a chromatic lament bass, a consolation in D-flat, the chord that will be the fugue's axis, Froberger's falling scale, and an ending on a lone B-flat, the fugue's first note.

pieces.title: Fugue XXII · Ma fin est mon commencement (23 voices)
pieces.notes:
'My end is my beginning': Machaut's rondeau of that title is a palindrome. This is a tombeau for Bach as a crab fugue for twenty-three voices: the second half is the first half played exactly backwards, in every voice. It begins with one alto on B-flat; the voices enter one by one in four choirs; all twenty-three sound together at the axis, the exact middle (between bars 48 and 49), on a diminished chord over an F pedal; then the retrograde takes them away in reverse order, and the piece ends on the same lone B-flat.

The subject joins the head of Bach's five-voice B-flat-minor fugue in Book I (BWV 867) to B-A-C-H, designed so that, read backwards, it ends with a cadence. Writing counterpoint that is correct in both directions is the hard part: a suspension played backwards is a different figure, and V-I becomes I-V; the rules used are set out in the notes. At the axis the subject sounds in augmentation with its H on the turning point, with the subject at normal speed in two tenors and three voices tolling F. The tempo and dynamics are palindromes too.

Listen for the exposition coming back reversed in the last minutes.

groups.name: Pair XXIII · B major (new, twenty-four voices)

pieces.title: Prelude XXIII · A Ground upon Ut re mi fa sol la
pieces.notes: Divisions on a ground in the manner of the English virginalists (Byrd, Bull): the six-note hexachord ut-re-mi-fa-sol-la repeats as a ground while the figuration gets quicker, plainsong, quavers, the ground moved to the treble, semiquaver runs, and a short close.

pieces.title: Fugue XXIII · Fantasia ut re mi fa sol la per tutti i tuoni (24 voices)
pieces.notes:
Around 1610 John Bull wrote a keyboard fantasia in which the hexachord ut-re-mi-fa-sol-la is carried as a long-note cantus through all twelve pitch levels, an experiment that only works if every key is usable, a century before Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier proved the point. Here twenty-four voices stand for the twenty-four keys: each voice sings the hexachord once, in long notes, in its own key, rising for a major key and falling for a minor one, in the order of keys of Bull's fantasia (checked in the 1899 Fitzwilliam Virginal Book edition), transposed to B.

In the exposition the B voice sings the hexachord in breves while the subject enters over each note in that note's key. Then a tour through eleven major/relative-minor pairs, as mirror canons, each pair carrying a subject entry in its key. At the summit the subject and its mirror sound in stretto over G-sharp-minor breves in the bass, arriving in B.

Try this: switch the temperament to meantone and listen to bars 66-71 (A-flat major / F minor), which open on a bare A-flat–E-flat fifth in six voices. In quarter-comma meantone that fifth is the 'wolf', 38 cents too wide, the reason keyboard players before Bach could not use every key; in Bach-Lehman it is a pure fifth.

groups.name: Pair XXIV · B minor (new, twenty-five voices)

pieces.title: Prelude XXIV · Preludio per i 24 tuoni
pieces.notes:
The cycle's farewell, and the doorway to its last fugue. Bach's B-minor prelude in Book I is a trio over a walking bass; this one walks through all 24 keys in the Well-Tempered Clavier's own order, two bars each: 48 bars, for 'the 48'.

In each key one of the upper voices quotes the opening of Bach's Book I fugue in that key, at Bach's own pitches, all 24 checked against the scores. The order holds a gift: each major key turns into its parallel minor, and each minor key's Neapolitan chord becomes the next major tonic, so the tonics climb by semitones from C to B, the twelve notes of Fugue XXIV's subject. In bar 44 the bass spells B-A-C-H. The prelude slows from bar 45 and stops on F-sharp major, whose A-sharp the fugue's first note resolves.

pieces.title: Fugue XXIV · twenty-five voices
pieces.notes:
Bach ends Book I with a B-minor fugue whose subject uses all twelve notes. This subject does the same: three dotted 'leans' and a chromatic climb, ending on the leading note. Its exact mirror is also twelve-tone.

The voices gather one at a time over 41 bars: exposition, a mirror stretto (subject against its own inversion), a dominant pedal over which the heads of Fugues V and VIII appear, and the subject in two-fold augmentation in the bass. At bar 43 the 25th voice, the contrabass, enters with the subject at quarter speed, and over it the subjects of Fugues V, VIII, II and IV each arrive at the point where the cantus's note makes their own key a harmony. After the arrival on B major, Fugue V's subject returns in B major, Fugue I's stretto ladder climbs once more, the subject's and the mirror's tails close in on one B, and all twenty-five voices gather on the last chord.

Wherever a voice could only have doubled another at the unison, it rests: at the convergence about ten to fourteen independent lines sound at once, and all twenty-five are heard together only on the last chord.

groups.name: Appendix · canons and contrapuncti (new)

pieces.title: Contrapunctus permutationum (4 voices, 24 keys)
pieces.notes:
Four lines written in quadruple invertible counterpoint: a cantus on B-A-C-H in half notes, a sighing line of suspensions, a walking eighth-note line, and a spinning sixteenth-note figure. Any of the four can be the bass. A script proved all 24 vertical orderings clean, in major and in minor.

The movement uses every ordering once, one in each of the 24 keys, going round the circle of fifths with each major followed by its relative minor. The orderings follow the change-ringing method Plain Bob Minimus, so B-A-C-H walks down and up through the four staves like a bell working through a peal.

The climax is statement 13 in F-sharp major, with B-A-C-H in the bass, followed by a sudden hush in E-flat minor. In the coda B-A-C-H is augmented and its last note, H (B natural), finally resolves to C.

pieces.title: Canon cancrizans per motum contrarium (table canon)
pieces.notes:
Two players read one page from opposite sides of a table. The second voice is the first played backwards and upside down, so the whole score turned through 180 degrees is the same piece. It begins in A minor and ends in C major, mirrored around D, the hinge note sounded in unison in bar 17.

A sarabande, then a double in sixteenths, the hinge, the double rotated, and finally the ground of the Goldberg Variations, which the second player arrives at simply by reading the first player's line upside down and backwards.

pieces.title: Canon per tempora · Four clocks, one hour
pieces.notes:
One melody at four speeds at once, in the ratio 4:3:2:1, bass slowest, voices an octave apart. The melody opens with the Westminster Quarters, so each new entry (bars 1, 9, 17, 25) is another clock beginning to chime, each faster than the last.

The entries are staggered so that all four clocks strike the final E at the same instant in bar 33. Bach's augmentation canons use only the ratio 1:2; no single player could perform four tempi at once.
